meaning: A company, organization, subsidiary, unit, project office, or other owner of operational knowledge.
avoid: company, organization, office, unit (these are kinds of node)

meaning: The stable id of a node. It never changes and is never reused.
A level of the hierarchy that holds one or more nodes.
The position of a layer in the hierarchy. Layer 0 is the top.
The subject area a node works in, such as transport or water.
A node whose internal structure is not modeled. It appears as one black box.
The whole tree of one organization's layers and nodes. It is the aggregate that guards the tree rules: one root, each layer one below its parent, and no children under a terminal node.
The record of every layer: its number, its name and role, its member nodes, and its transfer rule.
Which layer a node belongs to. It follows from the node's parent: the parent's layer plus one.
A read-only lookup that says whether a node exists and whether it is terminal. Code checks a node id through it, never by comparing strings.
A controlled source of knowledge, such as a document, profile, project report, or issue answer.
avoid: document, file, record (a document is one kind of item)

meaning: The stable id of a knowledge item, such as D10. It never changes and is never reused.
One specific version of a knowledge item. An update adds a version and never deletes an old one.
The unchangeable id of a version, such as v2.
The version of an item that retrieval uses by default. Our rule: exactly one per item.
A small, retrievable piece of a knowledge version, used by RAG.
Structured data about a knowledge item or an issue, such as node, type, or confidentiality.
The field of activity, confidentiality level, and allowed usage range of a knowledge item.
A SHA-256 fingerprint of a file's bytes or of its normalized text. Equal fingerprints mean equal content.
The kind of file a knowledge version was read from: Markdown, plain text, DOCX, DOC, or PDF.
Where a chunk comes from: the item, the version, the file, the pages, the heading path, and the character span.
The rule for cutting a version into chunks: the chunk size and overlap in words, and whether a chunk stays inside one section.
Knowledge that repeats other knowledge. Exact means the same content, near means almost the same. A partial repeat is an overlap.
Reading the text and its structure (headings, pages, tables) out of a file, with a parser or, for a scan, with the LVM.
Registering a file as a new knowledge item or a new version: detect the format, extract the text, record the metadata, chunk, and store.
Two documents in different items whose text is almost the same, for example a copy with a few words changed.
A part of one document that also appears in another, while the two documents as a whole differ.
One finding that two versions in different items repeat each other: the kind (exact, near or overlap), a similarity score, and the evidence.
The settings of duplicate detection: the size of a word group and the similarity limits for a near duplicate and an overlap.
Where a chunk is in its life cycle: created, embedded, checked for duplicates, or indexed.
A short machine-written note of what changed between a version and the one registered before it.
Two texts with a human label (exact, near, overlap or different), used to measure duplicate detection.
A DOCX or PDF made from a case-study Markdown source, named in the manifest's `real_file` column.
A PDF whose pages are only pictures, with no text layer, like a scan.
The text a PDF stores, which a reader can pull out without a vision model.
A PDF with both text pages and scanned pages, read page by page.
The normalized form of a question from a user or the system, used to search.
avoid: prompt (a prompt is the whole text sent to the model)

meaning: How close a chunk is to a query in vector or hybrid retrieval.
A link from a claim in an answer to its source: the file, and when known the chunk and page.
A problem, question, need, research gap, or operational concern modeled inside one node.
An issue derived from a parent issue, with its own status and relationships.
How far an issue has come, from 0 to 100, calculated by fixed rules.
A person, team, unit, or organizational capability that can help solve an issue.
The graph of typed relationships between issues, knowledge, and executors, such as "issue depends on knowledge". Short form: IKE model.
A hole in a node's knowledge: nothing relevant, outdated, conflicting, not answerable with confidence, or a judge score below the threshold.

Where an issue stands, one of the ten values of proposal 14.1: new, analyzing, knowledge identified, executor identified, solution proposed, in progress, awaiting decision, solved, unsolved, archived. Only the moves in a fixed table are allowed.
What kind of issue it is: a problem, a question, a need, a research gap or an operational concern.
How soon an issue should be worked on: not set, low, medium or high (a working scale until the supervisor decides).
A label that groups related issues inside one node, such as data or capacity. It is not the node's field of activity.
A blocked-by link: one issue waits for another issue of the same node. The links never form a cycle.
Where an issue stands among the issues of its node: its parent, its position among its siblings, its sub-issues, what blocks it, what it blocks, and the issues of the same category.
One of the seven things proposal 14.1 counts as progress, such as sub-issues defined or a solution proposed. Each is done or not done; sub-issues solved is a share.
One whole-number weight per progress factor, adding up to 100, read from config/issue_progress_weights.csv. The values are untuned.
Ranking the existing issues of the same node by how much they resemble a draft: shared words after stopwords are removed, and embedding similarity from Phase 8. There is no threshold yet.
A new issue that is not saved yet, in the node where it would live. It is compared with the existing issues.
One existing issue of the same node that resembles a draft, with its score and the words they share.
A small common word, such as the or on, that is removed before two texts are compared.
A sub-issue that the language model proposes. It becomes a SubIssue only when a person accepts it, as it is or edited.
Prepared knowledge sent from a lower layer to the layer above.
How detailed a package is: executive, managerial, technical summary, or detailed technical.
A layer's requirements for what it receives: topics, detail level, required fields, minimum judge score, maximum length, citation level. It is set per layer in the layer registry.
One run of a node's processing: find changes, re-index, update issues, build and judge a package. A trigger starts it.
The structured score from the LLM judge, with pass or fail and an explanation.
The scoring framework the judge applies, worth 20 points in total.
The minimum accepted score, such as 18 out of 20.
A named rule that turns how well one component works into a number, such as the share of questions answered correctly. The proposal calls it an indicator.
avoid: indicator, KPI, score (a score belongs to the judge)

meaning: The value of a metric on the simplest working version, measured before any tuning. Later versions must beat it.
The value a metric must reach to count as good enough. It is agreed with the supervisor, and only after a baseline exists.
avoid: goal, pass mark, threshold (a threshold is the JudgeThreshold)

meaning: The written rule that decides whether one answer to one answer-key question is correct. It gives the same result on every run.
A rule that must hold on every run. It is checked as pass or fail, not measured as a percentage. Example: a node never uses another node's documents.
A simple stand-in for a real part in a unit test, such as a stub that returns a fixed answer in place of the LLM.
avoid: mock, dummy (these are kinds of test double)

meaning: A test question kept apart from the answer key. No tuning step may read it; it is run once, at the end of Phase 14.
A versioned prompt with blanks, one per task type, kept in a registry.
A record of the local models in use: their task, limits, and evaluation notes.
A local model that turns a piece of text into a list of numbers, so that texts with similar meaning get close lists.
The local large language model that writes answers and summaries from retrieved chunks. The judge also runs on it.
The local vision-language model that reads page images, such as a scanned document, and returns text. Reading text from an image (OCR) is one of its tasks.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits so the file is smaller and runs faster, at a small cost in quality. Shown as Q4 or Q8 in model names.
A request for proposals that the system writes to invite solutions to an unsolved issue.
A submission that answers an RFP and is evaluated against it. In prose, call it an RFP response.
avoid: bid, offer; "proposal" alone for the project document

meaning: A structured report on a proposal: strengths, weaknesses, missing requirements, and a recommendation.
